transcript: when you're trying to figure out if right now is a good time to revive a certain piece of theatre there's a lot of different ways that you can approach the question but for a play like this I think some of the most important questions that you can ask are (a) will it reach a new audience? (b) will the existing audience be more ready and willing to hear what the play has to say than they were before? and (c)is the commentary still applicable and even better is it applicable in an additional or different way? I think this Broadway revival of David Henry Hwang’s Yellowface starring Daniel Dae Kim kind of does all three of those at the same time at certain points it's wrestling with questions that have become in some ways even more relevant than they were 20 years ago and at other times it's honestly a little bit of an “I told you so” about issues that we’re very well aware of now but were not talked about nearly enough back then and then on top of that I'm utterly fascinated by this play not just as an entertaining, meta, satire (which it is) but also as kind of a piece of performance art it's honestly kind of exhilarating how brazenly he uses the theater just as a platform for his own perspective not to preach at us necessarily but just to say his peace he's putting the cards on the table about his role in certain events in his life and at times painting himself in not a very flattering light but he's taking ownership of the narrative and it's a very stark reminder of just how powerful a writer's voice is it reminded me of something out of like an ancient public forum where a writer is just like “hear ye! hear ye! I have something to say and I'm gonna get you all in a room and I'm gonna say it and entertain you while I'm at it!” but it also fits the theme of like fiction versus reality the face you show versus the face you hide but either way it's honestly just fun to see him be so unapologetic about it and like for example the play is not about the Miss Saigon casting scandal but he does talk about it in the first few scenes and even just in those first few scenes he is naming names and showing receipts and like talk about still applicable: like Cameron Mcintosh is still a very powerful figure in the theater industry and still doing a lot of shitty things Jonathan Pryce is still a very well respected actor he's naming names of like respected journalists and Bernard Jacobs who has a theater named after him again most of the play is not talking about that I mean it's highly relevant but most of the play goes off into other directions that I don't wanna spoil cause I think it's fun to discover it as you go but it's just an example of what I'm talking about in terms of deciding to revive a show when it's going to hit the ears of the audience in a very particular way at that moment
